#214293. Trump pardons turkeys but Hill influence isn’t all gravy after midterm roasting

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1263 w)

Trump pardons turkeys but Hill influence isn’t all gravy after midterm roasting

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1263 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • President Donald Trump, first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson are all smiles at the annual Thanksgiving turkey pardon at the White House.
  • It has been revealed that president Donald Trump on Tuesday celebrated what he called one of the “immense powers” of his office, pardoning two turkeys ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday.
  • Joined by first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., set to lose power in January after he hands the gavel to a Democratic successor, Trump for the sixth time spared the long necks of two American turkeys — this time “Feathers” and “Freedom.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President Donald Trump, first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson are all smiles at the annual Thanksgiving turkey pardon at the White House. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images).

It has been revealed that president Donald Trump on Tuesday celebrated what he called one of the “immense powers” of his office, pardoning two turkeys ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. But lawmakers say his influence on Capitol Hill has already changed since Republicans’ midterm losses.

Joined by first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., set to lose power in January after he hands the gavel to a Democratic successor, Trump for the sixth time spared the long necks of two American turkeys — this time “Feathers” and “Freedom.”.

“In a few moments, under the immense powers vested in me by the Constitution of the United States of America, I will grant a full, absolute and unconditional pardon — meaning they will live forever — to two magnificent Thanksgiving turkeys, special turkeys,” Trump said, suggesting he could extend his power to spare the birds from the holiday dining table to somehow grant them immortality.

In a recent development, while voters punished his party’s candidates for doing too little to address high prices and his decision to join Israel in going to war with Iran, Trump on Tuesday remained focused on another area of largely unchallenged authority — his White House projects. He began the event by touting the yearly event, for the first time, being held on the helipad he had built on the White House’s South Lawn. Later, he confirmed intends for another new location next year.

“I'm told that per the long-running tradition, these exquisite animals stayed overnight at the nearby Willard Hotel. Unfortunately, for 200 years, the White House lacked appropriate accommodation to host such distinguished guests,” he said of the turkeys. “I'm pleased to announce that next year we'll be able to have a special location right over there in that rather small ballroom being built. It's going to host a lot of people and a couple of turkeys next year. We're going to do it inside.”.

Trump also highlighted that the two bright, white turkeys were raised in West Virginia — which he carried more than 40 points when he was on the ballot. The turkeys, now spared, will spend their remaining years in Texas, a state where Democrats scored two of their most high profile wins in the House and Senate races — something Trump left unmentioned.

Sources indicate that the pre-holiday vibes were lighthearted on Tuesday, with the president slated to later travel to South Florida for a Thanksgiving weekend of turkey and time at one of his golf clubs. But when he returns, lawmakers will continue assessing how much sway he still has on Capitol Hill as he begins what, for his predecessors, were their lame-duck eras.

One Republican Senate ally acknowledged his influence with lawmakers already has changed.

“I think it's going to be policy-to-policy on that,” said Senate Republican Conference Vice Chair James Lankford.

Recent findings suggest that “But he's the president of the United States all the way to the very end. So he still has his veto pen,” the Oklahoman added. “He still has the ability to be able to direct agencies to engage. We're passing legislation. It takes three to tango: House, Senate, and the White House.”.

Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz of Texas mentioned Trump’s influence, once the Democrat-controlled House and Senate are seated on Jan. 3, “will, obviously, be different.”.

“I don't think the incoming Democrat majorities are interested in passing productive legislation and passing pro-jobs legislation,” mentioned Cruz, a potential 2028 GOP presidential candidate. “I think, instead, they're just going to attack the president all day long.”.

Still, Cruz predicted “the president will continue to lead.”.

Recent findings suggest that trump on Monday highlighted how he likely intends to use his lame-duck influence on and off Capitol Hill when he successfully pushed for the reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. During an interview with CNBC’s Eamon Javers, Trump made an admission that would be stunning from any other sitting American president about a private company, saying he had been “speaking to the board directly and indirectly.”.

In a recent development, in a Monday statement, Nvidia stated its board had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

Industry observers note that such unprecedented moves are a big reason why Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., last week said he expects Trump to be Trump — despite overseeing a midterms campaign he insisted be about himself and his unpopular second-term record.

“Any president is going to have a lot of influence because they get to run the executive branch,” mentioned Scott, a former Sunshine State chief executive. “And they have the biggest pulpit in the world. So he's going to continue to have a lot of influence.”.

Still, some Republican lawmakers have criticized Trump and his team for what they call recent stumbles.

According to recent reports, sen. Jim Banks of Indiana last week told reporters he had “a lot of questions” about how Trump and his administration handled upgrades to the country’s air traffic control system that prompted a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13.

It has been revealed that “Somebody needs to be held accountable for what happened,” he remarked, raising concerns about the president demanding $50 billion in additional taxpayer monies to build a newly introduced system. “I’m not fully convinced that throwing out more money is going to solve the fundamental problems.”.

Trump also has taken ample friendly fire on social media from GOP members over his interference in the Huang scandal.

North Carolina GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan took to X to say the Nvidia founder’s reinstatement was “a mistake.”.

According to recent reports, “For the past two years, I have privately noted there is no way Jensen Huang can argue for the exportation of advanced American chips to China without being compromised. Turns out, well, we all know,” Harrigan wrote after Trump contended an administration probe had “exonerated” Huang of any potential wrongdoing. “There may come a time when forgiveness is warranted, but there are still too many unanswered questions and too much unmitigated risk. Today’s coordinated action between the manufacturer and this administration is likely to whitewash this risk.”.

Harrigan, a rare Tar Heel State Republican incumbent to win another term, echoed other GOP lawmakers in calling for an in-depth congressional probe in the Huang scandal and his affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative.

Next week could offer an early test of other Republicans’ willingness to break more publicly with Trump on certain complications, as Huang is scheduled to appear before multiple congressional committees.

Even before Trump threw his political weight behind Huang’s return, Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia said he had sensed a GOP president who had lost clout with his party’s Senate conference.

“I think the Nvidia issue has caused some major concerns about the Trump China policy, obviously,” Kaine remarked. “That is definitely creating some anxiety.”.

Trump has given clues that he is as concerned with his influence among the incoming Democratic majorities.

According to recent reports, “If they want to get things done, I want to get things done, too,” Trump said during a Friday press conference at the White House. “You know, there are those that say we might get more done because we had some Republicans that were just impossible to deal with.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Fox News Digital spoke to Defending Education senior communications director Erika Sanzi about Pritzker’s decision to opt out of a Trump administration tax credit funding Illinois student scholarships through a federal school-choice initiative.

Illinois Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker, widely believed to have presidential aspirations in 2028, is facing pushback from conservative education and school choice advocates over a move to opt out of a Trump federal scholarship tax credit program. Critics say the decision was made based on politics and not student outcomes.

Pritzker announced Tuesday that the state will opt out of the Trump administration’s Federal Scholarship Tax Credit program, refusing to allow Illinois students to receive scholarships funded through the federal school-choice initiative.

In a press release, Pritzker argued that participating in what he labeled a "school voucher program" would siphon money and attention away from public education while subsidizing donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation or other characteristics.

GOV KATHY HOCHUL SIGNS NEW YORK ONTO TRUMP'S SCHOOL CHOICE PROGRAM DESPITE TEACHERS UNION OPPOSITION.

"At a time when public school education needs investments more than ever, we should not siphon money from public schools for private education — especially as the Trump Administration’s policies decimate education," Pritzker wrote.

"We have a responsibility to do right by all of our students. Taxpayer funding should not subsidize donations to private schools that could discriminate based on religion, sexual orientation, or other characteristics.".

Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker holds a news conference in Chicago, Wednesday, June 24, 2026, to sign the Reproductive Health Records Privacy Act (HB 5295) into law. (Terrence Antonio James/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images).

Prominent conservative education activists and groups lambasted the move on social media, making the case that opting in takes nothing away from public schools and that Pritzker’s refusal simply blocks Illinois students from receiving privately funded scholarships while sending Illinois taxpayers’ charitable dollars to students in neighboring states.

Many also pointed to abysmal test scores in Illinois and noted that Pritzker is siding with the state's powerful teachers unions.

"It is a remarkably tone-deaf moment from Governor Pritzker, just before Thanksgiving, to deny 1.9 million K-12 students in Illinois access to life-changing educational resources as families are faced with rising costs and an affordability crisis," American Federation for Children CEO Tommy Schultz noted in a press release.

"Make no mistake: The Education Freedom Tax Credit could have unlocked needed resources for families and students, but Governor Pritzker chose to let those resources go to other states.".

Schools for America Executive Director Jane McEnaney wrote on X, "Imagine being Governor of Illinois and hating Donald Trump more than you care about the educational opportunities of 1.9 million kids.".

PROTECTING FAILING SCHOOLS AND SUPPORTING TEACHERS UNIONS IS NOT A WINNABLE STRATEGY, CEO WARNS.

Students raising hands while teacher asking them questions in classroom. (iStock).

Pritzker's decision comes after three Democratic governors — Latest York’s Kathy Hochul, Colorado’s Jared Polis and New Mexico’s Michelle Lujan Grisham — agreed to enter the program, saying it brings millions of dollars in additional educational support to students without taking a single cent from public school or state budgets.

It has been revealed that the U. S. Department of Education responded to Pritzker’s press release as well, posting on X that by opting out of the program, Pritzker "just handed scholarship dollars from generous Illinois taxpayers to students in other states instead.".

Department of Education official Greg Dolan also weighed in on X, saying "the only true thing in this whole statement from @GovPritzker is his name.".

"May it live in infamy for so callously and cruelly turning his back on helping students in need," Dolan added.

Erika Sanzi, senior director of communications at Defending Education, told Fox News Digital in an interview that Pritzker’s move was "unconscionable" and a "slap in the face" to parents, who will still be able to write off the taxes. But the money will not go to programs and resources for their children or other students in their state.

In a recent development, A Department of Education sign is displayed outside of their federal student aid office on July 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images).

It has been revealed that "You don't have to like the program, but can you at least describe it honestly and accurately?" Sanzi noted about Pritzker’s statement. "They smear it as a voucher program because vouchers is the scary word but, like, putting aside the merits of vouchers, it's not a voucher program.

Recent findings suggest that "You can stay in the school you're in and still take advantage of these services. That's not a voucher program. I wish I could tell you I was surprised by Governor Pritzker. I am not, but I do think it's disappointing. And I certainly have seen outcry from families in the state that are just extremely frustrated not only by his decision, but by what he said in relation to his decision.".

Fox News Digital reached out to Pritzker’s office for comment.

The state's major teachers unions praised Pritzker’s move. Chicago Teachers Union and Illinois Federation of Teachers President Stacy Davis Gates applauded the governor for rejecting what she called "Trump's voucher scheme," arguing that "public dollars belong in public schools" and saying the program would pull money out of public education with "zero oversight.".

Illinois Education Association President Karl Goeke similarly thanked Pritzker for rejecting vouchers, calling them a "scam" that sends public money to private schools lacking the same testing standards as public schools.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

With year-end best-of lists about to arrive, one strong contender for film of the year might seem unlikely at first: a five-hour, two-part, largely French-language biopic of French general and statesman Charles de Gaulle that only recently reached U.S. screens. Directed by Antonin Baudry and starring a strikingly de Gaulle-like Simon Abkarian, this French blockbuster comes with an almost-American budget of 74 million euros, one of the largest in the history of francophone cinema. Perhaps unsurprisingly given its subject, it became the hit of the French summer, offering audiences a nostalgic vision of national greatness at a moment of paralysis and division.

More surprisingly, the de Gaulle diptych has won praise outside of France as well, helped by the fact that it works superbly as both action and entertainment. Epic in scale, beautifully shot, both wryly amusing and often touching, its twin installments pass far more swiftly than their daunting runtime might suggest. There are clear contemporary echoes, too, in de Gaulle’s personal struggles and story of dogged European defiance. Indeed, it is not hard to see why viewers in France and elsewhere have warmed to this tale of an embattled European leader fighting to re-build sovereignty in the face of pressure from the United States as the moorings of a crumbling old order give way to something frightening and latest.

With year-end best-of lists about to arrive, one strong contender for film of the year might seem unlikely at first: a five-hour, two-part, largely French-language biopic of French general and statesman Charles de Gaulle that only recently reached U.S. screens. Directed by Antonin Baudry and starring a strikingly de Gaulle-like Simon Abkarian, this French blockbuster comes with an almost-American budget of 74 million euros, one of the largest in the history of francophone cinema. Perhaps unsurprisingly given its subject, it became the hit of the French summer, offering audiences a nostalgic vision of national greatness at a moment of paralysis and division.

It has been revealed that more surprisingly, the de Gaulle diptych has won praise outside of France as well, helped by the fact that it works superbly as both action and entertainment. Epic in scale, beautifully shot, both wryly amusing and often touching, its twin installments pass far more swiftly than their daunting runtime might suggest. There are clear contemporary echoes, too, in de Gaulle’s personal struggles and story of dogged European defiance. Indeed, it is not hard to see why viewers in France and elsewhere have warmed to this tale of an embattled European leader fighting to re-build sovereignty in the face of pressure from the United States as the moorings of a crumbling old order give way to something frightening and latest.

Industry observers note that each of the film’s two parts is just over two and a half hours long. The first, De Gaulle: Résistance (158 minutes; released in France as L’Age de fer), opens with the humiliation of the French collapse in June 1940. Refusing to accept the armistice, de Gaulle flees to England in a tiny plane. From there, he presses British Prime Minister Winston Churchill for greater support and builds a shaky government-in-exile from scratch, operating from a tiny office in central London.

The second, De Gaulle: Liberté (159 minutes; J’écris ton nom in France), covers 1943 to the end of 1944, following both the actions of the Resistance and de Gaulle’s power struggles with rival claimants to French leadership, before moving on to D-Day and the liberation of Paris. The epic closes movingly on Armistice Day, when Churchill visits the freed capital as de Gaulle’s guest.

According to recent reports, for audiences outside France, some of this will be familiar, from de Gaulle’s defiant broadcasts on the BBC to his haughty and stubborn personal affect. Undeniably imperious and quite unable to forget a slight, Abkarian’s de Gaulle is both a model of determination in the face adversity and, to the Allied leaders who bankrolled him, a quintessentially French pain in the ass.

A still from De Gaulle: Résistance.Pathe Films.

Sources indicate that other episodes are less well known in the English-speaking world, however, even as they remain central to France’s own story of the war, from the British destruction of the French fleet at Mers-el-Kébir in July 1940 (to keep its warships out of German hands) to the epic battle at Bir Hakeim in mid-1942. Perhaps now more familiar to tourists as the name of a Paris metro station, Bir Hakeim saw 3,700 Free French soldiers and their African colonial troops hold an isolated desert fort in Libya against German Gen. Erwin Rommel’s Afrika Korps for more than two weeks. Fighting against overwhelming odds, their bravery allowed Britain’s Eighth Army to fall back to El Alamein and regroup, marking an eventual turning point in the wider war. Providing the first film with a dramatic 15-minute denouement, the battle proved that de Gaulle’s ragtag movement could fight as a real army, provided a much-needed fillip to Free French morale, and strengthened the general’s position as a legitimate and potentially successful French leader.

Although this is very much a major-budget war movie, much of its power lies, paradoxically, in its intimate portrayal of the quiet complexities of leadership. In the public mind, de Gaulle can often come across as a cartoonish figure, all stubborn resolve, frosty self-regard, and Gallic hauteur. Abkarian’s ramrod-stiff performance is magnetic and provides plenty of evidence of this. But it also offers something more human, portraying with affection de Gaulle’s strange mix of grandeur and loneliness. The first film dwells in particular on his isolation and frequent despair. Arriving in London as a defeated tank division commander and former undersecretary of war, de Gaulle has no army, no money, barely any staff, and little claim to legitimate leadership. His situation is often tragi-comic, as when he tries unsuccessfully to win over members of the French expatriate community at a drinks party, or when he attempts to address a British audience in a packed theater, only to walk off ashamed without saying a word. In one especially memorable scene, he weeps alone in the bath of his small, dingy flat. In many others he is disconsolate, close to losing hope, and tempted to give up.

Sources indicate that this most Gallic of films is in fact based on an equally epic book by a British academic: A Certain Idea of France, Julian Jackson’s 900-page biography, published in 2018. Reviewing it in the New Yorker, Adam Gopnik dwelt on the crippling weakness de Gaulle faced in 1940, and how he ultimately managed to think his way out of it via a mixture of imagination, self-belief, and obstinacy. De Gaulle depended “more on theatrical élan than did pretty much any other public man of his century,” as Gopnik put it. “No one has ever played a weaker hand more compellingly. His life was one long brilliant bluff.”.

It is this vulnerability, rather than the more familiar image of pigheaded strength, that likely appealed to French audiences, prompting a reassessment of his traditionally unbending image and the controversial Gaullist legacy it inspired. For all that, the film is also huge fun. Its action sequences are slickly executed and, unusually for a European production, come with plenty of exuberant, Hollywood-style explosions. But it works as entertainment above all because at its center is the double act of de Gaulle and Churchill, played by Simon Russell Beale, easily the best of the many actors who have attempted the role.

A still from De Gaulle: Liberté.Pathe Films.

The two men are endlessly frustrated by one another and an obvious study in contrasts: one reserved, austere, and abstemious, the other impulsive, theatrical, and alcoholic. Yet each recognizes in the other a wartime leader fighting to save his nation against massive odds, creating a certain fondness and clear mutual regard. Among their many fine scenes is a comic row involving translation. De Gaulle speaks poor English; Churchill’s French is comical but serviceable. As they argue, both men hear their respective interpreters diplomatically softening their words. Each leader throws his man out of the room in turn, preferring to fight out their differences in broken language. The grudging but sincere warmth between the two both humanizes the complexities of wartime leadership and provides the film’s emotional heart.

Industry observers note that some critics have accused director Baudry of playing fast and loose with history, mixing invented characters with historical leaders, among other sins against accuracy. Jackson, who acted as a consultant on the production, has written warmly in its defense: “My pavlovian historical pedantry – ‘no that is wrong, it didn’t happen like that’, ‘you have these events in the wrong order’, etc – was rapidly slapped down with the reminder that this was a film not a documentary.”.

Industry observers note that the film’s very French portrayal of the United States, with a Machiavellian President Franklin D. Roosevelt cast as a chief villain, is one obvious area of potential historical dispute. But it also provides the film with its drama. Curiously, Adolf Hitler is never seen and barely even mentioned, while few German soldiers even appear. Instead, the real antagonist is Roosevelt’s Washington, and the U.S. president’s mounting frustration with an upstart French exile who contributes little manpower to the war effort yet irritatingly demands to be treated as an equal and a great power. In this sense it has something in common with zombie movies, where the greatest danger often comes less from the outside menace and more from potential betrayal within the group of humans struggling to survive.

A still from De Gaulle: Liberté.Pathe Films.

In Roosevelt’s eyes, France had forfeited any claim to great-power status, while de Gaulle himself was merely an arrogant annoyance and obstacle to his prepares. This broader threat to French survival is embodied in a plan to create the Allied Military Government of Occupied Territories (AMGOT), which the film presents as a U.S. scheme to permanently dismantle and divide the country. In this vision, a liberated France would be run by U.S. and British administrators, much as occupied Germany later was. That AMGOT was never the fully formed plan for France the film suggests is almost beside the point. In one memorable scene, Churchill is shown a future map of Europe in which France has vanished, carved up into a “Fresh Wallonia” and other invented entities. In an act of covert friendship, he leaks it to de Gaulle; a rare act of British solidarity with the French over the Americans.

As exaggerated as the film’s version of the AMGOT plan may be—and Jackson concedes it is somewhat overplayed—the question of how to deal with a powerful United States runs throughout the film, giving it its most obvious modern resonance. In part this reflects a traditional and enduring Franco-British divide, with France seeking self-sufficiency and sovereignty while Britain prefers proximity and access to Washington.

To distract from runaway protests, the French president is making a show of independence on the world stage.

The film’s ideas have poisoned military thinking for centuries.

According to recent reports, on the eve of D-Day in June 1944, for instance, de Gaulle’s demands over his forces’ role in the coming liberation of France prompt another giant bust-up with Churchill, and one especially memorable exchange, recounted in de Gaulle’s own highly readable memoirs. “”Every time we have to choose between Europe and the open seas, we shall always choose the open seas,”” he recalls Churchill declaring. “”Every time I have to choose between you and Roosevelt, I shall always choose Roosevelt.”” From Churchill’s point of view, this was entirely sensible; Britain had no obvious alternative to a superpower’s existential support, and it would have been foolish to side with an exile liberation army possessing no resources of its own. Nonetheless, it was a line de Gaulle would go on to quote throughout his life: an emblem of British perfidy and deference to Washington.

In a recent development, late in the second film, in a scene set in November 1944, de Gaulle sounds out Churchill on a deeper Anglo-French alliance. Churchill declines because Britain must stay close to Washington. The portrayal feels both enduring but also clearly modern, depicting two exhausted European powers facing common adversity but still quite unable to choose to be full partners with one another.

Recent findings suggest that more than anything, the film brings to mind the modern predicament of embattled and weakened middle powers, trying to find their way in a world dominated by far larger and more chaotic forces. During World War II, Britain and France both still thought of themselves as great powers—in de Gaulle’s case almost absurdly so, given his limited circumstances. Yet both clearly lived at the mercy of others, be they Hitler’s marauding armies or the caprice of an indispensable but overbearing U.S. ally.

In a recent development, today European nations face a version of the same bind, struggling to rebuild sovereignty in a world dominated by superpowers increasingly willing to coerce and threaten them. The message of the film is clearly a comfortable one for French audiences: France was right all along about untrustworthy Americans, and about the need for strength and independence rather than reliance on potentially unreliable U.S.-led institutions like NATO. Nonetheless, here de Gaulle offers modern Europeans clear lessons on how to counteract weakness, via a mixture of political imagination, risk-taking, and—above all—a willingness to stand up to U.S. power from time to time.

Industry observers note that what most people understand as “Gaullist” policies are increasingly common far beyond France as our geopolitical order frays, not least intrusive industrial policies aimed at technological self-sufficiency. Ben Judah, a British author and former political advisor, has gone further, proposing a new agenda of “Anglo-Gaullism” inspired by the French leader’s mixture of interventionism and political élan. “[T]he genius of de Gaulle was to re-enchant through storytelling a nation that had utterly lost confidence in itself,” he writes. Europe could clearly use a little more of that Gaullist enchantment today.

It is almost a cliche to contrast the giants of World War II with the slighter figures of our own generation. Yet watching de Gaulle’s struggles, it is hard not to think of the supplication of modern leaders like Mark Rutte, NATO’s secretary-general, whose approach to U.S. President Donald Trump was memorably described by Susan Glasser of the Latest Yorker as “strategic self-abasement.” De Gaulle is often fairly criticized for a grandiose vision of French leadership that far outstripped France’s actual power, leading to unhelpful delusions of national grandeur fed by the vision of its grandest of leaders. Nonetheless, de Gaulle’s obdurate refusal to accept decline—and his determination that France should stand, as he put it, as a nation “in the front rank”—should serve as an inspiration to Europe’s leaders today. This, too, is the lesson of the two excellent films that bear his name: to hold a vision of national power and to will it obstinately into existence, even if only by learning how to play a bad hand well.

According to recent reports, james Crabtree is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a distinguished visiting fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, and the author of The Perimeter: America's Struggle for Primacy in the Pacific (forthcoming in January) and The Billionaire Raj: A Journey Through India’s Newly introduced Gilded Age. X: @jamescrabtree.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, JOSHUA A. SCHWARTZ is Assistant Professor of International Relations and Emerging Technology at the Carnegie Mellon Institute for Strategy & Technology.

How Fighting Weakens Washington’s Reputation—and Backing Down May Strengthen It.

Industry observers note that in mid-February, after the United States failed to get Iran to renounce its nuclear ambitions, U.S. President Donald Trump issued an ultimatum. The Iranian leadership had to make “a meaningful deal” with Washington. “Otherwise,” he remarked, “bad things happen.” Barely eight days later, the United States and Israel began the war against Iran that continues today.

Sources indicate that that war has been criticized on many grounds, but analysts have often overlooked the basic assumption about U.S. credibility that it has tested. There is a long-held understanding that the United States’ willingness to use force to stand up for its interests is essential to deterring future adversaries—and convincing them to give in to the kind of sweeping demands the Trump administration made of Tehran. As Elbridge Colby, U.S. undersecretary of defense for policy, stated in the early stages of the conflict, “I think both our friends and potential foes are seeing the prowess of the joint force and that also contributes to deterrence.”.

In a recent development, going back to the early years of the Cold War, the concept of credibility—a state’s perceived capabilities and its willingness to use them even at high cost—has played a central role in the decisions that led to and sustained many of the United States’ largest military campaigns. The need to bolster U.S. credibility was a key force driving Washington’s strategy in Korea and Vietnam in the mid-twentieth century, and it played an vital role in Iraq and Afghanistan during the so-called war on terror. American strategists today continue to assess foreign policy decisions based on how they might strengthen or weaken the country’s reputation.

Industry observers note that but as the results of the Iran campaign have shown, a decision to use force does not always strengthen deterrence. After nearly ten months of war, and the expenditure of billions of dollars of munitions, the United States appears little closer to achieving its objectives of definitively ending Iran’s nuclear threat and ability to project power across the region, let alone securing regime change in Tehran. Meanwhile, the war has badly depleted U.S. military resources that could be used elsewhere and has further eroded the American public’s willingness to support military interventions. Rather than sending a strong signal of U.S. resolve, the Iran war risks conveying the opposite message. Vice President JD Vance argued that the reason the Republicans lost the midterm elections was the Iran war, and government officials in Tehran have gloated that “Americans remarked no to war.”.

Sources indicate that in fact, the conventional wisdom that standing firm in a military conflict enhances a state’s credibility misses something key. As the U.S. wars in Vietnam and Iraq showed, a prolonged military campaign may leave the country more cautious about using force, and less willing to bear the costs, in the years that follow. Adversaries notice this. Given that prior efforts by the Trump administration to compromise with Tehran were criticized as “appeasement” by figures like former U.S. Vice President Mike Pence, Trump may be tempted to continue or even expand the Iran campaign. But by taxing U.S. capabilities and deepening war-weariness among the American public, escalation in Iran could instead lead Beijing and Moscow to question Washington’s appetite for future interventions.

Policymakers should be far more skeptical about using military force for the sake of demonstrating U.S. resolve, and they should be less averse to backing down. The Cold War competition with the Soviet Union convinced the United States to intervene in costly proxy wars that consumed enormous human and military resources for questionable gain, and now the strategic competition with China and Russia may do the same. These kinds of conflicts are precisely the ones that are likely to harm, rather than help, U.S. credibility. Instead of obsessing about its reputation for resolve, which it cannot control, Washington must refocus its attention on maintaining the military strength and capabilities it needs to deter its major adversaries. Sometimes the best way to preserve both the capability and the willingness to act in the future is to walk away from conflict in the present.

In a recent development, for decades, policymakers and scholars have treated a country’s credibility as the dark matter of international politics—a hard-to-measure attribute that is nonetheless enormously crucial for maintaining deterrence. In the 1960s, nuclear deterrence theorist and Nobel Prize winner Thomas Schelling went so far as to say that acquiring a reputation for resolve is “one of the few things worth fighting over.” In keeping with this, it has long been assumed that whereas standing firm communicates to adversaries and allies alike that a country is willing to run risks and bear costs to uphold its interests, backing down or seeking to compromise conveys the opposite. As a result, many U.S. leaders and strategists have drawn on the logic of credibility to justify the most hawkish policies toward adversaries: making maximalist demands, using force, and remaining in wars long past the point where their costs exceeded their benefits.

Vietnam was a case in point. When debating whether to send the first group of U.S. troops to Vietnam in 1965, U.S. Secretary of State Dean Rusk told President Lyndon Johnson, “If the Communist world finds out we will not pursue our commitments to the end, I don’t know where they will stay their hand.” Later, as the United States became bogged down in the war, Assistant Secretary of Defense John McNaughton went further, arguing in a formerly top-secret memo that the primary reason for continuing the Vietnam War was to maintain America’s “reputation as a guarantor” and “avoid a humiliating U.S. defeat.” According to this logic, 58,000 U.S. soldiers and likely over a million Vietnamese people were killed not because the outcome of the war was itself crucial to U.S. interests, but because Washington worried how others—especially the Soviets—would perceive it if it withdrew.

Since the Cold War, the same justifications have been used to push the country into, and to sustain, many other conflicts. This was especially true during the so-called Forever Wars the United States was drawn into after the 9/11 attacks. On the night of 9/11, U.S. Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld said, “We need to bomb something else [other than the relatively weak Taliban] to prove that we’re, you know, significant and strong and not going to be pushed around by these kinds of attacks.” The logic of credibility not only played a role in Washington launching the Iraq war in 2003 but also locked it into the conflict, even as the costs rose and the raison d’être for the war—weapons of mass destruction—turned out to be false. As President George W. Bush said in 2006, “If we were to leave before the mission is complete, it would hurt U.S. credibility.”.

Conversely, strategists have been quick to criticize U.S. leaders who backed down. During the Syrian civil war, many were concerned about the reputational damage to the United States when President Barack Obama declined to respond to the Syrian government’s use of sarin gas to attack a rebel-held suburb of Damascus, thereby violating a red line that Obama had previously declared. In 2021, many foreign policy hawks reprimanded President Joe Biden for withdrawing from Afghanistan and for waiving some U.S. sanctions on Russia’s Nord Stream 2 pipeline project. At the time, Michael McCaul, the top Republican on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said, “U.S. credibility from Kyiv to Taipei cannot withstand another blow of this nature.” More recently, Trump himself has been accused of backing down against China on tariffs, which some have decried as another example of “Trump always chickens out,” or “TACO.” In each of these cases, critics argued that Washington’s failure to act has compromised the perception that the United States is willing to run risks and bear costs to achieve its objectives.

Despite the persistent assumption that U.S. credibility requires using force and refusing to back down, that thinking has been repeatedly challenged over the past decade. For one thing, experience has shown that a country’s past behavior may be a poor indicator of its present-day resolve. In April, for example, The New York Times reported that Trump believed that Iran was unlikely to attempt to close the Strait of Hormuz based on its past actions—such as its failure to mount a robust response to the U.S. and Israeli bombing of its nuclear facilities in the 12-day war in 2025. In reality, however, Iran has been far less restrained than expected in the current conflict and moved quickly not only to close the strait but also to attack U.S. allies and U.S. military bases across the region. In other words, Tehran’s failure to stand firm in 2025 had little bearing on its resolve in the present war.

In any case, it is far from clear that a country’s reputation for resolve is something that it can control by its actions alone. As Keren Yarhi-Milo has explained in Foreign Affairs, “credibility is in the eye of the beholder.” Even if a state acts decisively to signal strength, an adversary may not interpret that action as reason to reconsider its behavior. For example, despite Washington’s intention to communicate high resolve by bearing tremendous costs in the Vietnam War, the North Vietnamese Communist Party Central Committee concluded in 1965 that “the domestic situation in the United States, however, will not allow them to fully utilize their economic and military power in their war of aggression.” In other words, Hanoi ignored the intended signal from Washington and refused to back down.

It has been revealed that other pitfalls are associated with demonstrating resolve by standing firm and fighting. At the extreme, a state that leans too much on military strength can gain a reputation for aggression in ways that undermine long-term deterrence. Napoleonic France and Nazi Germany both had strong reputations for resolve, but their offensive actions ultimately provoked other countries rather than deterring them. There is certainly a risk that U.S. actions under the second Trump administration—such as decapitating the Iranian government and threatening to annex Canada, Gaza, and Greenland—could similarly backfire. For example, there is growing evidence that U.S. allies and partners in Europe, the Middle East, and Asia are rethinking their reliance on the United States and are seeking other sources of security. Far from conceding to Trump’s demands, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has described a “rupture” in relations between Washington and Ottawa and advocated for middle powers to band together to protect their sovereignty.

Even if using force bolsters a country’s reputation for resolve, it may harm the country’s broader credibility. For instance, Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine and its willingness to absorb hundreds of thousands of casualties since then has sent a strong signal about its resolve. Yet its dramatic underperformance on the battlefield against a far smaller and less well-equipped army has likely diminished the international perception of its military effectiveness. The war in Iran could similarly tarnish the United States’ military reputation. Since February, Washington has depleted at least half of its precision-strike missiles and advanced air defense interceptor missiles. It will likely take years to replenish these stockpiles given slow manufacturing times for so-called exquisite platforms. In the meantime, the United States has fewer advanced systems to draw on if China makes a move against Taiwan or if Russia attacks Poland or Estonia. For both Russia’s and the United States’ military campaigns, then, the net effect has been to reduce rather than enhance the countries’ reputation for military capability in the eyes of their respective adversaries.

Sources indicate that quite apart from the negative consequences that often come with decisions to use force, there is an even more fundamental problem with conventional thinking about credibility. In practice, backing down can actually be more helpful to a country’s reputation for resolve than fighting. This becomes especially clear in looking at the long-term effects of engaging in military interventions. Although the United States was victorious in World War I, the conflict produced a lingering war-weariness among the U.S. public and key policymakers. In the years after the Armistice, Americans expressed strong support for the idea that the United States should stay out of any future European war, a sentiment that was ultimately codified in the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s. Only after Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in December 1941, more than two years after war began in Europe, did the United States enter World War II. Fighting in World War I sent a signal of strong resolve to adversaries, but Americans’ war-weariness and resurgent isolationism in the years that followed conveyed that the United States would be less resolved to fight.

Recent findings suggest that this dynamic has been even more apparent in the aftermath of major U.S. wars since then. Following the Vietnam War, President Jimmy Carter declared that “young Americans should never again be sent to die in battle unless our own nation is endangered.” Consider how this kind of thinking affected adversaries’ view of the United States: In deciding to invade Kuwait in 1990, Iraqi dictator Saddam Hussein assumed that the United States was intensely casualty averse and might not intervene or would back down swiftly. General Wafiq al-Samarrai, Iraq’s head of military intelligence during the Gulf War, said in a 1996 interview that Saddam “thought that America’s involvement in Vietnam had badly damaged its willingness to use military power.” Although the Vietnam War was primarily fought to buttress the United States’ reputation for resolve, it had the opposite effect in practice.

According to recent reports, and again, during and after the U.S. war in Iraq, Americans became skeptical of costly military interventions. As a result, recent administrations have been especially hesitant to commit ground troops in combat operations. Iran is undoubtedly aware of this so-called Iraq syndrome, which may embolden Tehran to act more aggressively without having to fear a large-scale American ground operation.

Sources indicate that there is also experimental evidence that backing down may strengthen a country’s long-term reputation for resolve. In a survey I conducted in 2021 with 100 British parliamentarians, respondents were randomly divided into two groups. The first group read about a situation in which a hypothetical country backed down from a prior conflict. The second group read about a hypothetical country that stood firm in a prior conflict but displayed the same signs of war-weariness or “syndromes” that emerged in the United States after the Vietnam and Iraq wars. Both groups were then asked to estimate the likelihood that the country in question would stand firm or back down in a current dispute with the United Kingdom. On average, parliamentarians believed that the country that backed down in the prior dispute would have greater resolve in the current dispute. In other words, if fighting leads to war-weariness, then backing down can actually be better for a state’s future credibility.

As the U.S. campaign in Iran has demonstrated, choosing to fight to maintain a reputation for resolve is an incredibly risky gamble and may backfire. To avoid repeating the same mistake, U.S. policymakers and strategists need to rethink the relationship between credibility and fighting. First, the United States should avoid fighting altogether when the primary objective is shoring up reputation rather than defending a core national issue. If a conflict directly involves key security and economic interests, as did the U.S. Revolutionary War and World War II, then fighting can be a logical choice, assuming the United States has sufficient military capabilities to win the war at reasonable cost. But if the primary argument for the war relates to future credibility, as in Vietnam, then policymakers should be wary.

According to recent reports, second, if Washington determines that an adversary must be confronted with military force, then it must focus on limited, achievable objectives. Wars that drag on because they have much larger aims, or are prolonged simply for reputational reasons, may erode the country’s credibility by draining munitions and making Americans more reluctant to fight in the future. The two U.S. interventions against Saddam Hussein’s Iraq illustrate this point well. In the limited 1991 Gulf War, the United States rapidly expelled Iraqi forces from Kuwait at low cost and before war-weariness could set in among the U.S. public. But the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, in which Washington pursued the far more expansive goal of regime change, continued for years at high cost and made many U.S. policymakers and ordinary citizens alike less supportive of using force in the future.

In a recent development, finally, policymakers should focus less on the U.S. reputation for resolve, which they cannot control, and more on the country’s military capabilities, which they can. To deter Beijing and Moscow, Washington needs to convince both adversaries that it has the ability to prosecute a modern great-power war. The problem is that, although the United States continues to have the most advanced military capabilities and weapons systems in the world, they are limited in quantity, extremely expensive, and take a long time to replace. In the course of just a few months of fighting against Iran, the United States depleted huge percentages of its advanced and expensive stockpiles of offensive and defensive missiles.

Recent findings suggest that this alarming shortfall raises upcoming questions about whether the United States could sustain a longer war of attrition of the type Russia and Ukraine are fighting. Washington urgently needs to replenish its stockpiles and rethink its dependence on a small number of exquisite systems. It also needs to avoid costly conflicts that distract it from the principal threats it faces from China and Russia. Rather than making U.S. credibility stronger in the eyes of the world, continuing the war in Iran could well undermine it, just as fighting in Vietnam and Iraq did.

Three Routes to VPP Revenue for Installers, EPCs, and Developers Utility programs, wholesale markets, and bilateral contracts each come with different eligibility rules, payment structures, and commercial responsibilities.

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (592 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Solarpowerworldonline

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in June 2026, Google and Voltus confirmed a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM.
  • The deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs.
  • In a recent development, utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Intersolar & Energy Storage North America.

Industry observers note that in June 2026, Google and Voltus confirmed a three-year agreement to unlock up to 100 megawatts (MW) of distributed capacity annually in PJM. Under Voltus’s Bring Your Own Capacity model, Google funds procurement while Voltus aggregates qualifying distributed energy resources (DERs) and compensates participating customers.1.

The deal is one of three distinct paths to earn revenue from DERs. Across the U.S., utility programs, wholesale electricity markets, and bilateral contracts each have their own eligibility requirements, payment structures and commercial responsibilities.

Utility programs and procurement.

In a recent development, utility programs offer an established pathway for compensating customers and asset owners who reduce demand, shift consumption or discharge stored energy during periods of grid need. Payments may be tied to enrollment, committed capacity, measured performance or a combination of these factors. Massachusetts, for example, offers residential battery customers $275 per kW of average summer performance through ConnectedSolutions2.

Beyond customer incentive programs, utilities also procure distributed flexibility through contracts to address local grid constraints or broader capacity needs. Unlike standardized incentives, these arrangements can establish specific delivery requirements and compensation terms, creating opportunities for developers and service providers to assemble and manage DER portfolios. During a July 2026 heat event, Green Mountain Power dispatched 90 MW of stored energy capacity, helping customers avoid an estimated $6 million in peak-related costs during one peak hour3.

Sources indicate that aggregated DERs can earn revenue from energy, capacity, and ancillary services in wholesale electricity markets, subject to regional market rules and resource qualification. Unlike utility-specific programs, wholesale markets can provide access to broader regional revenue opportunities and multiple grid services. For developers and installers, participation typically occurs through an aggregator or other qualified market participant rather than through direct market registration.

Recent findings suggest that while Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) Order 2222 established a broader framework for DER participation, uneven implementation across regional markets continues to constrain commercial opportunities for aggregated resources. Market access does not automatically translate into revenue, as individual resources must still meet qualification requirements and comply with market-specific rules. Upcoming York Independent System Operator (NYISO), for example, requires DER aggregations to meet minimum capacity and real-time telemetry requirements, which can increase participation costs and limit the economic viability of smaller resources.

Wholesale participation can also expose VPP portfolios to fluctuating market prices, performance obligations and restrictions on receiving compensation for overlapping services. In Texas, ERCOT’s Aggregate Distributed Energy Resource (ADER) pilot allows aggregated DERs to participate in wholesale energy and ancillary services markets, subject to qualification, telemetry, and dispatch requirements.

Bilateral contracts and emerging buyers.

Bilateral contracts allow utilities and large electricity consumers to procure distributed flexibility directly from aggregators and service providers. Growing interest from data center operators and other large energy buyers is expanding the potential market for VPP capacity beyond traditional utility programs. Unlike standardized programs, bilateral agreements can be tailored to a buyer’s specific needs, with negotiated terms for capacity, delivery periods, compensation, and performance obligations.

In a recent development, the appropriate route depends on existing customer relationships, market access, and the responsibilities each partner assumes. Developers and EPCs working on commercial storage projects may find opportunities through utility procurement or capacity contracts, while residential installers with established battery customer bases may be well positioned to incorporate VPP enrollment into utility programs. Wholesale markets can expand revenue opportunities through aggregation partners, and bilateral contracts can create opportunities to develop resources around specific buyer needs.

Recent findings suggest that fox News legal editor Kerri Urbahn analyzes President Trump's newly introduced executive orders targeting birth tourism and birthright citizenship, plus the legal battle with the ACLU and a Texas hospital settlement. Urbahn discusses the constitutional battles ahead.

A DC federal judge, previously dubbed by President Donald Trump as an "anti- Trump Hater," blocked Trump's second attempt to restrict birthright citizenship in a Wednesday ruling.

U.S. District Judge Christopher Cooper, who was recently in Trump's crosshairs after ruling against efforts to shut down the Kennedy Center for renovations and add Trump's name to the cultural institution, issued a 67-page ruling striking down an August executive order that barred U.S. -born children whose parents are suspected terrorists or gang members, or children born through surrogacy to foreign parents, from citizenship eligibility.

Cooper's ruling comes months after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's initial executive order, signed on his first day back in office. The order attempted to deny birthright citizenship to U.S.-born children whose mothers were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor green card holders.

WHITE HOUSE RIPS ‘ACTIVIST’ BIDEN JUDGE WHO UPENDED TRUMP BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP ORDER.

Recent findings suggest that demonstrators hold up an anti-Trump sign outside the U.S. Supreme Court in Washington, DC, on June 27, 2025, after the justices curbed nationwide injunctions in a case stemming from President Donald Trump's initial bid to end birthright citizenship. (ALEX WROBLEWSKI/AFP via Getty Images).

"As the Supreme Court has made clear, however, the President cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws," Cooper ruled.

Trump's second executive order was already partially blocked on Sept. 2 by U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman in Maryland, whose injunction protected U.S.-born children of mothers who were in the country illegally or temporarily and whose fathers were neither U.S. citizens nor lawful permanent residents.

Cooper's ruling expanded protections beyond that class to include additional children born to certain foreign government and international organization employees, parents deemed "alien enemies" by the administration and foreign parents who used commercial surrogacy services in the U.S.

Recent findings suggest that "The merits in this case are clear-cut. The Supreme Court has twice confirmed that all children born in this country are U.S. citizens, save only for the small handful who are not subject to U.S. law," Cooper wrote.

It has been revealed that in addition to the Supreme Court's June ruling in Trump v. Barbara, Cooper referred to the high court's ruling in United States v. Wong Kim Ark, which determined that a man born to Chinese immigrants was a protected U.S. citizen under the 14th Amendment.

SEN ERIC SCHMITT SEEKS TO END BIRTH TOURISM, REVOKE CITIZENSHIP FOR BABIES OF FOREIGN DIPLOMATS.

Brady Briefing Room at the White House in Washington, DC, on June 27, 2025, following a U.S. Supreme Court ruling on nationwide injunctions in litigation over his first birthright citizenship executive order. (Mehmet Eser/Middle East Images via AFP).

Cooper noted that Wong Kim Ark established narrow exceptions to birthright citizenship, including for children of foreign diplomats, children born aboard foreign public ships and children of enemy forces occupying American territory.

"While the Fourteenth Amendment may theoretically permit new exceptions beyond those listed in Wong Kim Ark, Congress has not authorized any such exceptions," Cooper wrote.

Cooper argued that membership in a terrorist organization alone does not satisfy the historical exception to birthright citizenship for children of enemy forces occupying U.S. territory. He criticized the Trump administration's contention that foreign invaders could occupy American territory without actually holding it as an "outside-the-box understanding" of what constitutes an occupation.

"To recap, a parent’s purported status as an alien enemy, standing alone, cannot strip a U.S.-born child of his right to birthright citizenship," Cooper wrote. "The alien-enemy exception, properly understood, applies only to children born to hostile enemy forces in temporarily occupied U.S. territory.".

Cooper also rejected Trump's attempt to deny birthright citizenship to children born through commercial surrogacy arrangements involving foreign parents, finding that the circumstances of their birth do not exempt them from U.S. jurisdiction.

Industry observers note that "Indeed, foreign parents choose surrogacy arrangements in the United States precisely to have the child be governed by U.S. law and have the surrogacy process ‘supervised by a court.," Cooper wrote.

TRUMP TO ASK SUPREME COURT TO REHEAR BIRTHRIGHT CITIZENSHIP CASE AFTER 'INSANE DECISION'.

He noted that, prior to Trump's second executive order, the State Department recognized the citizenship of children born on American soil regardless of whether they were born through surrogacy.

The Trump administration is expected to appeal the decision and request that the executive order be temporarily enforced while the litigation works its way through the courts, a process that could take months.

"This is just another ruling from an activist judge appointed by Obama attempting to thwart President Trump’s commonsense agenda," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis noted in a statement to Fox News Digital. "The birthright citizenship executive order is consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court.".

According to recent reports, the Justice Department could seek temporary relief from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the DC Circuit or seek intervention from the Supreme Court. Fox News Digital reached out to the Justice Department for comment.

In addition to ruling against Trump's Kennedy Center renovation efforts, Cooper ruled that Trump's Department of Government Efficiency must turn over records requested in a Freedom of Information Act lawsuit.

Trump has called Cooper one of the "Radical Left Democrats.".

Johnson banks on GOP unity as permitting bill vote nears

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Andy Harris, R-Md., on left, and Chip Roy, R-Texas, speaking, could be key to Speaker Mike Johnson's vote count on the GOP side.
  • The House will take up a Senate-passed bill to overhaul the federal permitting system under a rule when it returns next week, a House aide remarked on Tuesday.
  • According to recent reports, but it may come down to GOP attendance, with many departing members not showing up to vote in the days following the midterms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that reps. Andy Harris, R-Md., on left, and Chip Roy, R-Texas, speaking, could be key to Speaker Mike Johnson's vote count on the GOP side. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The House will take up a Senate-passed bill to overhaul the federal permitting system under a rule when it returns next week, a House aide remarked on Tuesday. The bill, which passed the Senate on Nov. 19 in a 62-33 vote, has the endorsement of President Donald Trump and a wide range of industry groups that are generally GOP allies. Adoption of the rule, typically a party-line affair, would almost certainly lead to final passage and Trump's signature.

According to recent reports, but it may come down to GOP attendance, with many departing members not showing up to vote in the days following the midterms. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., in a Nov. 20 letter to colleagues, implored them to come back to work next month to finish out the lame-duck session, citing the permitting bill vote among other things. But it remains to be seen whether defeated lawmakers will take him up on that.

And several Republicans, led by House Freedom Caucus members, have used their leverage in rule votes to extract last-minute changes to legislation from leadership.

In a recent development, last December, the House considered a bill to overhaul the National Environmental Policy Act from Rep. Jared Golden, D-Maine, and House Natural Resources Chairman Bruce Westerman, R-Ark. Ahead of the vote on that rule, Republicans including Freedom Caucus Chairman Andy Harris, R-Md., sought last-minute changes to portions of the bill they were concerned would allow offshore wind projects in the Atlantic Ocean to move forward. Westerman agreed, which in turn caused the American Clean Power Association to withdraw support for the bill.

In a recent development, harris hasn’t commented yet on the Senate-passed permitting measure. Nor has Freedom Caucus Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, who has called for permitting generally to be a lame-duck priority but was another one of the holdouts on Westerman’s bill last year. Still, the Freedom Caucus is generally on board with permitting legislation and specifically cited it as a priority for the session's waning days.

In a recent development, republicans are generally expected to support the bill, which enjoys backing from industry groups like the American Petroleum Institute, National Mining Association and Edison Electric Institute, which represents investor-owned utilities. The bill’s supporters go beyond the energy sector, including groups like the American Road and Transportation Builders Association and National Association of Home Builders.

And two Democrats — Golden and Rep. Marie Gluesenkamp Perez of Washington, both members of the Blue Dog Coalition — have taken the rare step of crossing the aisle to support Republican rules this year in order to move legislation they support. Both have issued statements that speak favorably of the permitting bill.

Senate Environment and Public Works Chairman Shelley Moore Capito, one of the bill's lead authors, was enthusiastic about the bill's chances in the other chamber.

Recent findings suggest that "I think there’s a real will there," the West Virginia Republican stated Tuesday after presiding over a pro forma session. "We’ve got to get enough Republicans there to vote, and I think that’s what the speaker is hoping to do. I think he wants to do it under a rule, it sounds like, but I’m very excited about it because I think it’s very, very doable.".

With the path through the House yet to be fully illuminated, a vote under suspension of the rules, which requires two-thirds of members present and voting to pass, remains an option. But that's a trickier path given the split among Democrats.

The Senate-passed bill emerged from that chamber in a weaker position than advocates anticipated earlier this month, when 73 senators backed advancing it on an initial procedural vote.

It has been revealed that after opponents got through with the measure — including an amendments blockade by Oregon Democratic Sens. Jeff Merkley and Ron Wyden that left backers unable to incorporate changes necessary to shore up support — there were just 62 "yes" votes, although there were four absent GOP supporters.

Just 15 out of 47 Democratic caucus members voted for it, including only one member of the Environment and Public Works panel — Rhode Island’s Sheldon Whitehouse, who wrote the bill with his GOP and Democratic counterparts on EPW and Energy and Natural Resources.

If there is full attendance on both sides, the threshold for passage on suspension would be about 290 votes. Permitting bill supporters would need about one-third of House Democrats to vote in favor — 71 with current vacancies — similar to their level of Senate Democratic support, assuming all Republicans were on board.

That doesn’t seem out of the question given that the leadership of the 112-member-strong Fresh Democrat Coalition has expressed support led by the current chair, Brad Schneider of Illinois; the incoming chair, fellow Illinoisan Nikki Budzinski; and Scott Peters, D-Calif., chair of the coalition’s Environment, Climate and Clean Energy Working Group. So has the centrist Blue Dog Coalition.

Clean energy groups like the Solar Energy Industries Association and American Clean Power Association back the bill, as do key labor unions including the AFL-CIO, Laborers’ International Union of North America and International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. The AFL-CIO sent a legislative alert on the bill, which indicates it may include the measure on its annual legislative scorecard.

It has been revealed that but Rep. Jared Huffman, D-Calif., ranking member of the House Natural Resources Committee, is a firm “no” on the current bill. He offered a series of changes on Monday needed to win his support — which have negligible chance of acceptance by the bill’s authors or by Trump, who last week noted the bill would put money “back in the pockets of hardworking Americans” and lead to “tremendous amounts of latest building.”.

Sources indicate that huffman wants to roll back proposed limits on Endangered Species Act reviews as well as the bill's 150-day limit on judicial challenges and “project certainty” protections intended to bar future administrations from revoking approved permits. Huffman noted the certainty protection would legislate “a third term for Trump” by preventing future administrations from revoking permits for projects that could have detrimental environmental impacts, such as fossil fuel or mining projects.

Meanwhile, the official position of the nearly 100-member Congressional Progressive Caucus is opposed. And the House Sustainable Energy and Environment Coalition remarked it couldn’t support the Senate bill without changes, arguing the measure “includes environmental rollbacks that are concerning to us.”.

Two influential Democrats on energy and climate complications came out against the measure in its current form this week — Reps. Sean Casten of Illinois and Mike Levin of California, who are among the SEEC’s vice chairs. Casten and Levin have worked together on legislation intended to overhaul the transmission permitting system and address energy affordability.

In a statement Casten remarked the bill would make it “impossible” for a future administration “to undo the damage being done by the Trump Administration’s willful disregard of current environmental law and judicial precedent,” adding he would vote "no" on the Senate-passed bill “with confidence in our ability to craft a better version in the 120th Congress.”.

Casten, who co-founded a clean energy startup before coming to Congress, is at the moment challenging House Financial Services ranking member Maxine Waters, D-Calif., for the gavel next year, in a bid resting in part on his environmental bona fides, including sustainable investment and climate-risk regulation.

Levin, an environmental lawyer by trade, praised the bill’s provisions making it easier to build interstate transmission lines, a key bottleneck barring the development of more wind and solar power generation.

“These grid reforms are real, and there’s no guarantee a better bill comes along that can actually become law soon,” Levin stated in his statement. But he said it wasn’t worth the potential environmental costs, adding that “taking the current deal would mean giving up protections we may never win back in exchange for gains that aren’t guaranteed either.”.

Major environmental advocacy groups like the Sierra Club and Natural Resources Defense Council have long been opposed to the measure, as have Native American tribes and representative organizations like the National Congress of American Indians.

Another factor affecting the debate in the House is how to handle a bipartisan package of Senate changes agreed to on both sides of the aisle, but blocked on the floor by Merkley, a staunch opponent of the bill.

That amendment included language making it more difficult to circumvent National Historic Preservation Act rules; giving landowners and state regulators more time to resolve disputes before eminent domain is invoked for transmission projects; and closing loopholes in the bill’s language aimed at making data center developers pay for their own electric-grid upgrades.

If that amendment had been included, the Senate vote count may have been higher. But attaching it in the House would send it back to the Senate for another round of votes, which may not be practical given the dwindling legislative session. An alternative would be to tuck the amendment into another must-pass bill, like government funding legislation or the National Defense Authorization Act.

The Newly introduced Democrat Coalition’s statement, while overall supportive, noted the group “will look for opportunities to negotiate changes that reflect environmental and Tribal concerns.”.

Senate Indian Affairs Chairman Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, and ranking member Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, worked on changes in the amendment to address concerns tribes and Native American organizations raised about the NHPA section.

“I'm not going to abandon it just because the bill has been passed now. So working it on the House side, looking for other opportunities to advance it yet this Congress,” Murkowski stated Nov. 20. “So we're not done.”.

Capito told reporters Tuesday that the permitting bill's fate has been invading her dreams.

"My husband Charlie wakes me up, I’m like in sleep going ‘huh, huh, huh.’ He goes, ‘What’s wrong? What’s wrong?’ I said, ‘I’m just dreaming about permitting reform,'" Capito recalled. "That’s kind of a sad state of affairs. It was our 50th anniversary.”.

Lauren Green, Jackie Wang and Jacob Fulton contributed to this report.
